No independent peer review is claimed. Pin checks provide technical evidence only.

old_row.rationale: The Egyptian invasion force includes Libyans and Ethiopians; the later prophetic rebuke also names Ethiopians and Libyans as a great force. These are different campaigns, and the source's horses and chariot counts are not transferred to Asa's battle.

new_row.rationale: The Egyptian invasion force includes Libyans and Ethiopians; the later prophetic rebuke also names Ethiopians and Libyans as a great force. These are different campaigns, and the source's horses and chariot counts are not transferred to Asa's battle.

changes.reason: Do not imply that the later Asa rebuke retrospectively refers to Rehoboam's Egyptian invasion.

old_row.rationale: The stolen gold shields are attributed to Solomon, whose earlier manufacture of large and smaller hammered-gold shields is recorded. The connection traces the royal gold armament without asserting that every described shield was carried off individually.

new_row.rationale: The stolen gold shields are attributed to Solomon, whose earlier manufacture of large hammered-gold shields and an additional set of gold shields is recorded. The connection traces the royal gold armament without asserting that every described shield was carried off individually.

changes.reason: The second shield set is not explicitly called smaller in the supplied target.

old_row.rationale: Abijah opens his address by calling Jeroboam and Israel to listen; its concluding warning again addresses Israel's sons and forbids fighting the Lord. These units mark the speech's audience and appeal.

new_row.rationale: Abijah opens his address by calling Jeroboam and Israel to listen; its concluding warning again addresses Israel's sons and declares that fighting the Lord will not prosper. These units mark the speech's audience and appeal.

changes.reason: The target warns that fighting will not prosper; it does not use an explicit prohibition.

old_row.rationale: Terror from the Lord comes upon the communities around Gedor during Asa's victory; the later account reports such terror among surrounding kingdoms after hearing the Lord fought Israel's adversaries. The different geographical extents remain distinct.

new_row.rationale: Terror from the Lord comes upon the communities around Gedor during Asa's victory; the later account reports such terror among all the kingdoms of the earth after hearing the Lord fought Israel's adversaries. The different geographical extents remain distinct.

changes.reason: Preserve the target's stated extent of all kingdoms of the earth.

old_row.relationship: Royal cult-removal comparison with differing details
old_row.rationale: Both describe Asa removing his mother from a religious or ruling role and burning her cult objects at the Kedron or Kidron watercourse. Chronicles names Maacah and Astarte; Kings names Ana and a grove gathering. The woman's identity and the differing objects are not reconciled.

new_row.relationship: Royal cult-removal comparison with differing details
new_row.rationale: Both place Asa's removal of his mother beside destruction by fire at the Kedron or Kidron watercourse. Chronicles names Maacah, ministry to Astarte, and an idol; Kings names Ana, leadership, a grove gathering, and her hiding places. This narrative comparison does not resolve the woman's identity or equate the differently described objects.

changes.reason: State the two accounts' objects and roles explicitly without treating hiding places as an equivalent cult image.

old_row.rationale: Both report Asa bringing silver, gold, and vessels into the Lord's house. Chronicles speaks of holy things of David and the house, whereas Kings specifies his father's and his own pillars; these object descriptions are preserved without harmonization.

new_row.rationale: Both report Asa bringing in silver, gold, and vessels. Chronicles describes holy things of David and of the Lord God's house; Kings explicitly gives the Lord's house as the destination and calls the objects his father's and his own pillars. The distinct object descriptions and wording about the house remain intact.

changes.reason: Do not assign the target's explicit destination to a source unit that calls the objects holy things of the house.

old_row.rationale: The Lord's eyes examining the earth to strengthen whole hearts corresponds to David's charge that the Lord examines every heart and should be served with a whole heart. The specific promise of military strength belongs to the source.

new_row.rationale: The Lord's eyes examining the earth to strengthen whole hearts corresponds to David's charge that the Lord examines every heart and should be served with a whole heart. Chronicles places this assurance of strength within the rebuke about Asa's reliance and coming war.

changes.reason: Distinguish the whole-heart strength statement from its surrounding military rebuke.

old_row.rationale: Jehoshaphat seeks the Lord in contrast to Israel's works. Asa's earlier rebuke supplies a specific failure to trust the Lord, explaining why the surrounding Jehoshaphat account qualifies the father's example as his earlier ways rather than endorsing every act.

new_row.rationale: Jehoshaphat seeks the Lord and walks in his father's commandments. Asa had expressly instructed Judah to seek the Lord and carry out the law and commandments, providing a concrete earlier paternal instruction corresponding to this conduct.

changes.reason: Replace an inferred explanation of the earlier-ways qualifier with the direct paternal instruction being followed.

old_row.rationale: Both Jehoshaphat passages connect terror from the Lord among surrounding kingdoms with freedom from attack or rest. The later passage explains it as a response to hearing of divine victory; the source does not give that immediate cause.

new_row.rationale: Both Jehoshaphat passages connect terror from the Lord with freedom from attack or rest. The source specifies kingdoms around Judah; the later passage says all the kingdoms of the earth and explains their terror by hearing of divine victory, a cause not stated in this source unit.

changes.reason: Preserve the different stated geographical scope in each passage.

old_row.rationale: The report of gifts from foreigners and livestock from Arabs extends the earlier notice of gifts from all Judah. The distinction between domestic and foreign tribute clarifies the narrative's picture of prosperity without identifying the foreign groups more narrowly.

new_row.rationale: The report of gifts from foreigners and livestock from Arabs extends the earlier notice of gifts from all Judah. The distinction between domestic and foreign gifts clarifies the narrative's picture of prosperity without identifying the foreign groups more narrowly.

changes.reason: The passages call the transfers gifts, not a formally defined tribute.

old_row.rationale: The roster gives Ednas 300,000 men from Judah, matching the numerical total of Asa's earlier Judah force. The kings, commanders, and occasions differ, so an identical military unit or unchanged force is not claimed.

new_row.rationale: The roster gives Ednas 300,000 men from Judah, matching the numerical total of Asa's earlier Judah force. The kings and occasions differ, and the earlier unit names no commander; an identical military unit or unchanged force is not claimed.

changes.reason: The earlier target names no commander, so no difference between named commanders can be asserted.

unresolved_candidates.reason: The proposed identity of Maacah daughter of Ouriel from Gabaon with Maacah daughter of Absalom is not established by these supplied-English units, despite the shared maternal connection to Abijah. The conflicting father descriptions remain unresolved. The retained regnal-summary comparison with 1 Kings 15:2 does not resolve this identity.

The prophecy is attributed to Adad in the source, whereas the chapter opens with the Spirit upon Azarias son of Oded. This review does not identify Adad with either Azarias or Oded or repair the attribution. The retained reform comparison does not depend on resolving the prophet's identity.

The source calls Asa's mother Maacah; Kings' regnal notice calls his mother Ana daughter of Absalom. Their personal identity is not resolved here. The retained comparison with the cult-removal narrative in 1 Kings 15:13 preserves its named woman, role, and objects without identifying the women independently.

editorial_notes.note: All actual source units and exact canonical references were retained in their supplied order. Meaningful same-chapter connections identify list functions, royal succession, speech framing, explicit narrative explanations, and prediction/outcome relations; none claims independent identity verification.

Numerical, chronological, personal-name, object, agency, and wording differences are stated rather than repaired. The 1 Kings 12:24y-24z suffix target is preserved. Asa succession remains at 2 Chronicles 13:23 and his evaluation at 14:1. The supplied accurate-aim wording of the royal wounding is retained.
